item.title: Seruiratu says the people come first, not power, not privilege, not the interests of a few
Fiji deserves a better way of governing - NextGen Alliance Party Leader
item.description: Fiji deserves a better way of governing. That is the message from NextGen Alliance Party Leader Apisai Moce as he officially launched the party at Rewasau Village, Nabobuco in Naitasiri.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji deserves a better way of governing.

That is the message from NextGen Alliance Party Leader Apisai Moce as he officially launched the party at Rewasau Village, Nabobuco in Naitasiri.

Moce says the NextGen Alliance Party was not created because Fiji needed another political party, but because the country deserves a better way of governing.

He says governments have changed, Prime Ministers have changed and policies have changed, yet too many ordinary families continue to face the same struggles year after year.

He says the time has come to stop asking which political party is in power and start asking whether the government is truly working for the people, stressing that the government exists for only one purpose, which is to improve the lives of its people.

Addressing young people, Moce says too many believe their future begins at the airport, adding that the NextGen Alliance wants them to see opportunities at home and build their future in Fiji.

He also says every citizen, regardless of ethnicity or background, belongs in Fiji's future and that the country's success depends on what unites its people rather than what divides them.

Moce says the party's priorities include honest government, strong families, quality education, accessible healthcare, safe communities, prosperous farmers, growing businesses, meaningful jobs, modern infrastructure and stronger rural and maritime development.

He also says leadership is about service rather than power, adding that it is not about status, titles, motorcades or power, but about walking beside the people, listening before speaking and serving before commanding.

The NextGen Alliance Leader says if the people of Fiji entrust his party with public office, it will remember that Parliament exists to serve villages, government exists to serve families and leaders exist to serve the people.

He also highlighted the party's grassroots beginnings, saying it has no wealthy backers or powerful interests behind it and was built by ordinary Fijians, including market vendors, farmers, families, church members and young volunteers.

item.title: Cancer stigma and myths are putting children's lives at risk - Ali
item.description: Myths and misconceptions about childhood cancer are preventing some children from receiving life-saving treatment, according to WOWS Kids Fiji board member Anabel Ali, who is urging communities to end the stigma surrounding the disease. Speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, Ali highlighted that the organisation has come across families and communities that discourage or even
item.content:encoded:
Myths and misconceptions about childhood cancer are preventing some children from receiving life-saving treatment, according to WOWS Kids Fiji board member Anabel Ali, who is urging communities to end the stigma surrounding the disease.

Speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, Ali highlighted that the organisation has come across families and communities that discourage or even prevent children diagnosed with cancer from seeking medical treatment.

Ali says while adults have the right to make decisions about their own healthcare, children depend on their parents and caregivers to access treatment.

Ali says delaying or refusing treatment can shorten a child's life and reduce their chances of recovery.

She says there is a misconception that a cancer diagnosis automatically means death, but many children can recover and go on to live normal lives if the disease is detected early and treated promptly.

Ali says WOWS Kids Fiji is currently supporting 64 children battling cancer across Fiji, including 43 boys and 21 girls , with a 10-month-old baby being the youngest child receiving support.

She says they have lost five children since January this year and see around 30 new childhood cancer cases annually.

She adds that the number of children affected by childhood cancer could be even higher, as some cases may be managed directly through hospitals or private healthcare providers.

Ali is urging communities to talk openly about childhood cancer, recognise the early warning signs and encourage families to seek medical attention as soon as possible, saying early diagnosis and access to treatment give children the best chance of survival.

item.title: Tooth decay affecting 8 in 10 five-year-olds in Fiji - Ravunawa
item.description: Almost eight out of every 10 five-year-old children in Fiji are already experiencing tooth decay, with the Ministry of Health reminding children that brushing their teeth twice a day can help protect their health, confidence and future. Speaking at the National Tooth Brushing Day celebrations at Queen Victoria School, Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa highlighted that oral health has
item.content:encoded:
Almost eight out of every 10 five-year-old children in Fiji are already experiencing tooth decay, with the Ministry of Health reminding children that brushing their teeth twice a day can help protect their health, confidence and future.

Speaking at the National Tooth Brushing Day celebrations at Queen Victoria School, Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa highlighted that oral health has a direct impact on children's daily lives, including their ability to enjoy food, concentrate in class, attend school and smile with confidence.

Ravunawa says by the time students reach the ages of 12 and 15, about half are affected by cavities, while nearly 90 percent of teenagers with tooth decay have not visited a dentist for treatment.

He says poor oral health during childhood can have long-term effects, noting that many older Fijians are missing an average of nine teeth, with some having lost all their natural teeth.

Ravunawa says the Government wants to change this trend by encouraging children to develop good dental habits from an early age.

He says the Ministry of Health, schools and partners such as Colgate-Palmolive are working together to improve children's oral health through dental screening, protective sealants and fluoride treatments.

Ravunawa reminded students that the key message for National Tooth Brushing Day is simple: brush for two minutes, twice a day, once in the morning after breakfast and once at night before going to bed.

He says students should use fluoride toothpaste to help keep their teeth strong and healthy.

He also acknowledged the support of Colgate-Palmolive, saying the company's contribution of toothbrushes and fluoride toothpaste is helping put the power of a healthy smile directly into the hands of Fiji's children.

The Assistant Minister says the Government remains committed to ensuring every child in Fiji, including those living in remote and maritime communities, has access to clean water, toothbrushes and proper dental care.

He encouraged schools, families, communities and corporate partners to work together to ensure every child in Fiji grows up healthy and smiling.

item.title: Study finds weak implementation continues to affect children with disabilities
item.description: One young person quoted in the report summed up the challenge, saying, "We can write all the policies. It can be beautiful and all. The implementation is the issue that I've seen." The report also highlights positive steps, including efforts by some organisations to give children with disabilities opportunities to take on leadership roles, speak up on issues affecting them, and improve the collect
item.content:encoded:
One young person quoted in the report summed up the challenge, saying, "We can write all the policies. It can be beautiful and all. The implementation is the issue that I've seen."

The report also highlights positive steps, including efforts by some organisations to give children with disabilities opportunities to take on leadership roles, speak up on issues affecting them, and improve the collection of disability data.

Despite those efforts, the study found that several major challenges remain, as there is not enough funding to implement policies effectively, responsibilities are often unclear, and many Government agencies and organisations still lack awareness of the needs and rights of children with disabilities.

The report also found that information on children with disabilities is often incomplete and not shared effectively between agencies, making it more difficult to identify gaps in services and provide the support families need.

It says children with disabilities and their families are often not consulted on decisions that affect them, while communication barriers continue to prevent many children from having their voices heard.

item.title: Fiji-born entrepreneur brings Australian skin health expertise to Fiji
item.description: A Fiji-born entrepreneur has fulfilled a dream more than 20 years in the making by bringing advanced skin health treatments from Australia to Fiji. Speaking during the opening of The Verve Lounge Fiji - Skin Health at TappooCity in Suva, founder Feriel Ali says it has always been her dream to return home and introduce specialised skin health services to Fijians.
item.content:encoded:
A Fiji-born entrepreneur has fulfilled a dream more than 20 years in the making by bringing advanced skin health treatments from Australia to Fiji.

Speaking during the opening of The Verve Lounge Fiji - Skin Health at TappooCity in Suva, founder Feriel Ali says it has always been her dream to return home and introduce specialised skin health services to Fijians.

Ali says The Verve Lounge is different from a beauty salon or spa because it focuses on improving skin health by treating the deeper layers of the skin.

She says the Suva clinic will introduce advanced treatments that are not widely available in the Pacific, including new skin regeneration technology aimed at improving long-term skin health.

Director Amit Biswas says the business has also been working with local partners to help train Fijians and develop the skills needed to deliver specialised skin health treatments.

Biswas says finding the right people and investing in modern equipment have been some of the biggest challenges, but there has been strong interest from Fijians wanting to learn and work in the industry.

He says the company also plans to introduce more advanced treatments in the future as it continues to expand its services in Fiji.

Biswas has encouraged aspiring entrepreneurs to pursue their dreams, saying building a business takes time, investment and determination, but people should not wait if they believe in their vision.

item.title: Style Fiji aims to double funds raised for charity tonight
item.description: Style Fiji organisers are aiming to double the funds raised for charity this year as they prepare to launch the 2026 edition of Fiji's largest charity fashion and entertainment event. Speaking ahead of the Style Fiji 2026 launch, which will take place this evening at the Sheraton Fiji Golf & Beach Resort in Denarau, Nadi, committee member Samson Lee highlighted that the event will provide sponsors
item.content:encoded:
Style Fiji organisers are aiming to double the funds raised for charity this year as they prepare to launch the 2026 edition of Fiji's largest charity fashion and entertainment event.

Speaking ahead of the Style Fiji 2026 launch, which will take place this evening at the Sheraton Fiji Golf & Beach Resort in Denarau, Nadi, committee member Samson Lee highlighted that the event will provide sponsors and supporters with greater transparency on how funds are used while unveiling this year's theme and charity beneficiaries.

Style Fiji is an annual charity fashion and entertainment event that raises funds for local health and community organisations, including the Fiji Cancer Society and the Spinal Injury Association of Fiji.

Lee says the launch has been organised primarily for sponsors, major supporters and long-time guests, with around 100 to 130 people expected to attend.

He says the evening will provide a breakdown of how last year's funds were spent, introduce the committee's chosen charities for 2026, and allow guests to pre-purchase tables and tickets for the main event .

Lee says this year's launch marks a new direction for Style Fiji, as last year's gathering focused mainly on the transition following the handover of the event.

He says the charity event is now in its 15th year and has continued to be held at the Sheraton Fiji Golf & Beach Resort after moving from Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa to provide more space and improved parking for guests.

He says although Style Fiji is known for its glamorous fashion showcase, its heart has always been charity.

Lee says last year's event raised $50,000 , and the committee's goal this year is to double that amount .

He says launching the campaign earlier will help build excitement, strengthen support and give sponsors more time to get involved.

Lee adds that tonight's event will also provide an opportunity for sponsors, business leaders, tourism industry representatives and influencers to network while learning more about the committee's plans for the 2026 event.
